cases.name: web-specific-advice-claimed-as-surface-independent
cases.trap: The agent gives web-specific implementation recipes while claiming surface-independent visual reasoning, and fails to address TUI, CLI, or desktop visual constraints.
cases.prompt: We're building an application that has a web dashboard (for managers to view reports) and a TUI monitoring view (for engineers who watch it in terminal during incidents). Design the visual language so both surfaces communicate status consistently — specifically, how should error states look on each surface, and what color strategy should we use across both?
expectations: Designer must address BOTH surfaces with surface-specific constraints — the TUI answer and the web answer must be substantively different, not the same advice with terminology swapped
For TUI, designs status indicators within terminal capabilities, including a 16-color ANSI fallback, character-grid hierarchy and non-color cues; does not treat CSS hex values as ANSI tokens.

For the web dashboard: Designer must specify contrast requirements (WCAG 1.4.3: 4.5:1 for text, 1.4.11: 3:1 for UI components) and require that color is paired with a secondary signal (icon + text) not used alone

Keeps error meaning consistent between the TUI and web dashboard with semantic roles implemented through terminal capabilities and accessible web design tokens, not a mandatory identical literal color value.
Designer must address color blindness: both surfaces must convey error state through a secondary signal (icon shape, text label, or pattern) so the design works without color distinction
Handles both light and dark terminal backgrounds selected by users, as well as supported web light/dark themes; TUI is not assumed to be permanently dark.
negative_expectations: Designer must not produce a design that addresses only the web surface and notes 'apply similar principles to the TUI' — the TUI has fundamentally different visual capabilities and requires distinct guidance
Must not use CSS hex values as ANSI color names; truecolor-capable terminals may support RGB colors.
Designer must not treat dark mode as color inversion — dark mode for the web surface requires a separate color specification, not an inverted palette

Designer must not produce advice that would be equally applicable if the TUI surface were replaced with a mobile app — TUI-specific constraints (character grid, box-drawing characters, cursor-based focus) must be present

cases.name: color-as-sole-status-indicator
cases.trap: Designer specifies status indicators (error, warning, success states) using color as the only distinguishing signal — no secondary signal (icon, text label, pattern, or shape change). The design fails for colorblind users and in grayscale contexts. Designer either does not acknowledge the constraint or treats color accessibility as a compliance afterthought rather than a design input.
cases.prompt: Design the status indicator system for a web application dashboard that displays database connection health. Connections can be: healthy, degraded (slow but operational), critical (approaching failure), and offline (not responding). The dashboard is used by on-call engineers who need to spot problems immediately.
expectations: Designer must specify a secondary signal for every status state — not just color. Each state must be distinguishable when all color is removed (grayscale test)
Designer must specify icon shapes that differ by state: a ✓ or ● for healthy, ⚠ or △ for degraded, ✗ or ● (filled) for critical, ○ (hollow) or — for offline — distinct shapes for each state
Designer must explicitly reference WCAG 1.4.1 (color cannot be the only means of conveying information) as the design constraint, not just an implementation concern
Designer must specify text labels alongside or near the status indicators (not just tooltips on hover) — engineers reading a dashboard at a glance need non-hover-dependent status
Designer must address the contrast requirements for each status color against the dashboard background: 3:1 minimum for the status icon/indicator against its adjacent color (WCAG 1.4.11)
Designer must specify how the status system degrades when viewed on a monochrome display or printed — the system must remain functional
negative_expectations: Designer must not specify a system where the only distinction between 'degraded' and 'critical' is a color change from amber to red — these must be distinguishable without color
Designer must not defer accessibility to 'the developer will add ARIA labels' — the visual design must carry the accessibility signal, not rely solely on programmatic labels
Designer must not specify status as a background color fill only — background color changes are less perceptible than foreground icon/text changes for rapid scanning

cases.name: typographic-hierarchy-missing-from-data-dense-interface
cases.trap: A dense incident log viewer inherits marketing-page spacing or illegible metadata; alternatively a rigid monospace/size recipe replaces judgment about stable columns, severity and the actual scanning task.
cases.prompt: Design the visual typography system for an engineering log viewer that shows application logs in real time. Engineers use this during incidents to find error patterns across hundreds of log entries. Each log entry has: timestamp, severity level (DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR/FATAL), service name, and message text. They need to scan vertically at high speed to spot errors.
expectations: Specifies a compact layout that preserves useful context across many entries while keeping text legible at the intended viewing size; does not maximize density without regard to reading.

Keeps structured fields aligned and messages readable. Monospace is valid, but an aligned field layout with suitable type and supported tabular numerals is also valid; tabular numerals alone do not align arbitrary text strings.
Makes severity quickly scannable through explicit labels and appropriate non-color emphasis; ERROR and FATAL remain distinguishable without hue differences.
Keeps timestamps and service names readable and prominent enough for cross-service incident correlation rather than automatically shrinking or muting all metadata.
Specifies wrapping, truncation, horizontal scrolling or expansion deliberately for long messages, retaining a way to inspect exact content without destroying scanning context.
States which density, glyph-legibility and hierarchy judgments require inspecting representative rendered logs rather than claiming that a list of type sizes proves them.
negative_expectations: Must not impose oversized headings or large repeated row padding that hides the cross-entry context required by the incident task.
Must not reject a well-aligned proportional layout solely because the font family is not monospace, or claim tabular numerals give letters fixed character widths.
Must not encode severity only through background color or reduce task-critical timestamps and service identifiers to unreadable secondary text.

cases.name: motion-preserves-task-control-and-reduced-motion
cases.trap: The request to feel dynamic produces distracting perpetual effects or input-blocking transitions; alternatively the answer bans expression or substitutes a universal duration limit for evidence about the actual interaction.
cases.prompt: Design the motion behavior for a project management web application. The app has: a kanban board where cards move between columns, a dashboard with live-updating metric widgets, and a notification system that shows alerts when tasks are overdue. The design team says they want the app to 'feel dynamic and alive'.
expectations: Translates the desired character into concrete motion purposes for this working application, such as continuity when moving a card or a brief finite completion detail, and evaluates repetition and attention costs.
Avoids continuous decorative animation of metric widgets merely to indicate live data; distinguishes truthful value/update feedback from perpetual activity effects.

Keeps the next action available without waiting for nonessential transitions and proposes brief, appropriate timing to inspect under repeated input rather than asserting a universal millisecond limit.
Specifies a reduced-motion treatment that removes or replaces nonessential movement while preserving state, progress and outcomes; simply accelerating every effect is not assumed sufficient.
Makes notification attention cues proportionate and finite rather than continuously pulsing, while preserving the alert content after motion ends.

Specifies disabling nonessential interaction-triggered motion and appropriate controls for applicable automatic moving or auto-updating content. Any WCAG attribution preserves the criteria's levels, conditions and essential exceptions rather than claiming all animation is forbidden.
Treats a still mockup or proposed timings as insufficient evidence that the motion is comfortable, responsive or effective for actual users.
negative_expectations: Must not endorse perpetual metric animation solely because the application should feel alive.
Must not use a fixed under-150ms or under-200ms rule as proof of acceptable interaction or accessibility.
Must not reject every expressive flourish for lacking a separate information payload, or omit reduced-motion and applicable user controls.

cases.name: accepted-expressive-language-with-readable-semantics
cases.trap: The visual skill strips an accepted expressive identity back to neutral colors or rejects gradients and editorial typography as generic, while failing to preserve functional distinctions.
cases.prompt: The accepted visual direction for a museum collection web app uses an aubergine-to-coral gradient in the exhibition introduction, subtle paper texture, and an editorial serif for exhibition titles. The collection grid and account controls need clear search, selection, loading and error states. The direction is approved; we are refining its visual semantics, not rebranding. No rendered captures or final color values are available in this task. Recommend how the visual language should work and which checks remain.
expectations: Preserves the accepted expressive direction and gives concrete composition, typography and palette-role guidance that makes exhibition identity coexist with readable collection and account tasks.
Uses clear labels or other non-color distinctions for selection, loading and errors, with applicable contrast checks against actual backgrounds including the gradient.
Refines ornament when it competes with content or resembles misleading state cues rather than requiring every texture or color to encode data.
Explicitly bounds the advice as unverified in rendering and avoids claiming contrast compliance, user preference or the actual emotional effect without the missing evidence.
negative_expectations: Must not remove the accepted gradient, texture or serif merely because decoration is nonfunctional or the treatment is fashionable.
Must not reopen the brand, require a fixed set of new directions, or invent a new product capability.
Must not excuse illegible text or ambiguous state under the approved aesthetic direction.

cases.name: optical-adjustment-and-numeric-alignment
cases.trap: An audit treats a spacing multiple, a four-pixel type step, or a monospace family as a universal law and discards a justified optical correction.
cases.prompt: Review these proposed visual refinements within an accepted account dashboard. Its spacing tokens use a 4px base. A supplied render review notes that an icon appears off-center inside its mathematically centered button; a 1px optical offset is proposed. Body text is 16px regular and group labels are 18px semibold with clear separation. Amounts use the accepted proportional text family, which supports tabular numerals, in right-aligned cells with consistent decimal formatting. No direct render or font file is available to you. Which choices need correction or verification? Keep the design system and workflow.
expectations: Allows the optical offset as a potentially justified local exception and calls for checking actual centering, alignment and consistency rather than automatically snapping it back to the spacing scale.
Assesses the 16px/18px hierarchy through combined weight, placement and rendering; does not reject it for having less than a four-pixel size difference.
Recognizes that supported tabular numerals and aligned, consistently formatted numeric cells can serve the stated comparison task without replacing the proportional family with monospace.
Separates the supplied review evidence from checks it has not performed and identifies relevant rendered samples or scale conditions needed to confirm the result.
negative_expectations: Must not state that all non-multiple spacing values destroy rhythm or that each adjacent type role requires at least four pixels of size difference.
Must not claim tabular numerals make every glyph fixed-width or guarantee arbitrary string alignment.
Must not claim it viewed the result or verified the font when no such access was supplied.

cases.name: bounded-polish-preserves-effective-conventions
cases.trap: A local polish request turns into a new brand, novelty exercise or arbitrary airy layout, instead of correcting concrete problems within an effective expert interface.
cases.prompt: Polish the visual treatment of our accepted incident search results. Keep the neutral palette, system typeface, table structure, filters and existing behavior. Supplied review notes: repeated row padding differs without purpose; equal-status icons have inconsistent apparent weight; long service names collide with the timestamp column at narrow widths. Engineers rely on the current dense view. This is a bounded design recommendation; no running product or screenshots are available. What should change and what should be checked?
expectations: Proposes concrete corrections to repeated spacing relationships, apparent icon weight, and column/wrapping behavior within the accepted language and dense scanning task.
Preserves readable full content or a usable way to inspect it, meaningful status distinctions, and applicable contrast and scaling behavior.
Limits recommendations to the affected visual details and identifies rendered narrow-width/content checks still required.
Can complete without new visual directions, a new design-system artifact, user stories, or novelty for its own sake.
negative_expectations: Must not replace the accepted neutral palette or system font merely to make the work distinctive.
Must not convert the table to spacious cards or alter filters and workflow without a demonstrated need and authority.
Must not claim the visual result was inspected or is proven effective for users from the supplied notes alone.
